newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's EMU drive gets boost from EU tax decision.
newsitem.headline: Italy's EMU drive gets boost from EU tax decision.

text.p: Italy's bid to secure a place at the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU) received a boost on Friday when Brussels approved the use of a one-off tax for Europe.

Eurostat, the European Union office responsible for overseeing government accounting practices, gave the green light to the "Euro tax" that Prime Minister Romano Prodi plans to levy this year in his drive to cut Italy's heavy budget deficit.

While few economists had expected a decision against Italy, approval was critical for the government's finances and its national and fiscal credibility, said Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London.

Italy's 1997 budget for 62.5 trillion lire ($37.6 billion) of deficit-cutting measures already included the 5.5 trillion lire Euro tax. It is a key element in Prodi's efforts to reduce the deficit to the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) needed to take part in EMU at its projected 1999 start date.

The European Commission says the part of the Euro tax in question counts for 0.19 percent of GDP -- a sizeable chunk in what economists estimate will be a deficit-to-GDP ratio of 3.5 to 3.8 percent this year if no extra budget measures are taken.

But while critical for Italy, Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets in Milan, pointed out: "The benefit on the budget deficit of these accounting adjustments has already been taken into account in the 62.5 trillion budget for whole year."
Instead, with the Eurostat decision out of the way, attention is focused on how tough Prodi can make an additional package of 1997 budgetary measures which he announced this week.
"The message from the supplementary budget is that it could increase chances that at the end of the year the deficit will be close to the 3.0 percent line," De Gregorio said.

Prodi said earlier this week the mini-budget would be "structural". Details will be announced in coming weeks once the government has seen state accounts due in March. But analysts are sceptical over what spending he can cut without initiating reforms to the pension, welfare and health systems.

The hard-left Communist Refoundation, which guarantees a majority in the lower house of parliament for Prodi's centre-left coalition, adamantly opposes pension reforms and says the mini budget must contain no spending cuts or new taxes.

Economists say however the strength of the government's determination to battle on with meeting EMU criteria is appreciated by financial markets and Prodi has received some encouragement this week from the opposition Freedom Alliance.

Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi proposed striking "a transparent compromise" with the government and establishing an "understanding for Europe" to help meet the EMU commitments while reforming Italy's welfare state.

Now analysts say Prodi must press on with bringing forward preparation of the 1998 and including the kind of structural adjustments expected both by the financial markets and by those EU partners which doubt Italy will be fiscally fit for EMU. ($ = 1663 Italian Lire)
